title: Square Roots of Negatives in Equations

steps.body: In Algebra 1, x² = −16 was a dead end: 'no real solutions.' Now you can finish it: x = ±√(−16) = **±4i**. Every equation of the form x² = −k has two purely imaginary solutions, ±i√k — the square-root method never stalls again.

widget.prompt: What are the solutions of x² = −36?

options.label: x = ±6
options.feedback: (±6)² = +36 — that solves x² = 36. The minus needs the i: ±6i.

options.label: x = 6i only
options.feedback: (−6i)² = −36 as well — squaring kills the sign, so both ±6i count.

options.label: x = ±18i
options.feedback: 18 is 36 ÷ 2 — take the square ROOT of 36: 6, so ±6i.

steps.body: See why a shifted negative square has no real crossing, then locate its complex pair.

widget.prompt: (x − 1)² = −4 is equivalent to y = (x − 1)² + 4 meeting y = 0. Build that parabola and inspect the x-axis.
widget.successFeedback: The vertex is (1, 4), so the parabola stays above the real x-axis. The equation still has the complex pair x = 1 ± 2i.
widget.shapeFeedback: Keep a = 1. This equation shifts the parent parabola without stretching or reflecting it.
widget.vertexFeedback: The equation is y = (x − 1)² + 4, so its vertex must be (1, 4).

predict.prompt: Before building y = (x − 1)² + 4, how many real x-axis crossings will it have?

options.label: None — its lowest point is above zero
One — the vertex lies on the axis

predict.reveal: The built graph bottoms out at y = 4, so there are no real crossings. In the complex plane, (x − 1)² = −4 gives x = 1 ± 2i.

steps.body: Shifted squares work the same way: (x − 2)² = −9 gives x − 2 = ±3i, so **x = 2 ± 3i** — a real shift plus an imaginary spread. The answers come as a matched pair, one +3i and one −3i around the center 2.

explanationVariants: x − 2 = ±3i, so x = 2 ± 3i — center 2, imaginary spread ±3.
Root the right side (±3i), then add 2 to undo the shift.

commonBuilds.feedback: The (x − 2) undoes with +2, not −2 — the center is +2.
√(−9) is imaginary: ±3i, not ±3 — the right side is NEGATIVE nine.
The 2 is the shift (real center) and the 3 comes from the root (imaginary spread) — they don't swap.

widget.missFeedback: Root both sides: x − 2 = ±√(−9) = ±3i, then move the 2 across.
widget.successFeedback: Right — root to ±3i, then shift back by +2.

options.label: x = 1 ± 5i
options.feedback: The +1 inside undoes with −1 outside: the center is −1.

options.label: x = −1 ± 5
options.feedback: The right side is −25, so the root is ±5i — imaginary, not ±5.

options.label: x = ±5i
options.feedback: That drops the shift — the (x + 1) moves the center to −1: x = −1 ± 5i.

explanationVariants: Move the 49 across, then root the negative: ±i√49 = ±7i.

widget.prompt: What are the solutions of x² + 49 = 0?

commonBuilds.feedback: (±7)² = +49, so x² + 49 would be 98, not 0 — the minus demands i: ±7i.
(−7i)² = −49 too — a quadratic hands you BOTH: ±7i.

widget.missFeedback: x² = −49 roots to BOTH values: ±√49 · i = ±7i.

explanationVariants: Checking a complex root works like any check: square it, watch i² flip the sign, add.

widget.prompt: Is x = 3i a solution of x² + 9 = 0?

options.label: yes — (3i)² = −9, and −9 + 9 = 0
options.feedback: Right — complex roots check by substitution just like real ones.

options.label: no — (3i)² = 9, and 9 + 9 = 18
options.feedback: (3i)² = 9i² = −9, not +9 — the i² flips the sign, and the check closes at 0.

options.label: no — you can't substitute imaginary numbers
options.feedback: Substitution works for ANY number — complex arithmetic handles the rest: (3i)² + 9 = 0. ✓

options.label: yes — because 3² = 9
options.feedback: The reason matters: it's (3i)² = −9 (note the MINUS) that cancels the +9.

explanationVariants: Move the 4 across first — the square equals NEGATIVE four, so the spread is imaginary.

commonBuilds.feedback: Root the 4: √4 = 2, so the spread is ±2i, not ±4i.
That solves (x − 5)² = +4 — here the square equals −4, so the spread is imaginary: 5 ± 2i.

widget.missFeedback: Isolate the square: (x − 5)² = −4, root to ±2i, then shift by 5.
widget.successFeedback: Right — (x − 5)² = −4 roots to ±2i; shift back by +5.

steps.body: x² = −k finally has answers: ±i√k, shifted by the square's center.
takeaways: x² = −k gives x = ±i√k — two purely imaginary roots.
(x − h)² = −k gives x = h ± i√k — real center h, imaginary spread.
Complex roots verify by substitution, with i² = −1 doing the work.
steps.teaser: Next: the quadratic formula meets a negative discriminant — and keeps going.

concept.body: x² = −k roots to ±i√k. For x² = −4: √4 = 2, so the solutions are ±2i.

explanationVariants: Root the 4 to get 2; the minus supplies the i.

widget.prompt: What are the solutions of x² = −4?

options.label: x = ±2
options.feedback: (±2)² = +4 — the negative right side needs i: ±2i.

options.label: x = ±4i
options.feedback: Take the ROOT of 4 first: √4 = 2, so ±2i.
